audits.question: Check the entry's divine-name writing/reading/register distinction against a located textual or scholarly source; retain textual-date and transmission limits, not a recovered universal ancient pronunciation.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/israel-ancient-hebrew.md section 6 'Tetragrammaton taboo' table rows 'Mishnah Sotah 7:6' and 'Later reading conventions' (lines 107, 109) with bullets at lines 111-114; also section 3 line 55 (Medieval Masoretic vowel and accent systems ... written notation much later than Iron Age inscriptions)
audits.entry_claim: The entry asserts, with transmission limits: (a) in later Jewish practice Adonai is the standard reading substitute carried by the Masoretic qere perpetuum, and Masoretic pointing cues that substitute rather than a pronunciation built from YHWH's consonants, so 'Jehovah' is not an independently recovered pronunciation; (b) Mishnah Sotah 7:6 contrasts Temple pronunciation of the name 'as written' with a spoken substitute outside the Temple; (c) the divine name was known in early rabbinic usage simply as 'the Name' (HaShem), an avoidance expression; (d) these are reception-layer evidence (Mishnah compiled c. 200 CE; Masoretic notation medieval), not documentation of tenth-century BCE speech or a recovered universal ancient pronunciation.
audits.source_citation: Mishnah, Seder Nashim, Sotah 7:6 - Hebrew text (unpointed, vowel-pointed, and Maimonides-codex versions displayed) with medieval commentaries, Hebrew Wikisource public-domain transcription
audits.source_locator: Sotah 7:6, mishnah proper, second sentence (both the unpointed and the 'mishnah menukedet' pointed version shown on the page)
audits.source_excerpt: בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ אוֹמֵר אֶת הַשֵּׁם כִּכְתָבוֹ, וּבַמְּדִינָה בְּכִנּוּיוֹ. ('In the Temple he pronounces the Name as it is written; in the province by its substitute.') [Hebrew; gloss this worker]
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL public HTTP GET of the Hebrew Wikisource page; full-page text extracted including the pointed and unpointed mishnah text and attached medieval commentaries (Maimonides, Bartenura glosses)
audits.basis: The entry's own anchor for the register row is Mishnah Sotah 7:6; this fetch supplies the actual mishnah sentence behind that row. The Maimonides gloss on the same page identifies the written form as yod-he-vav-he and the substitute as the form used today, and Bartenura glosses the substitute as alef-dalet-lamed (Adonai), matching entry claims (a)-(c) at primary-text level.
audits.coupling_implication: The write/speak/place register split is documented as a stated rabbinic distinction with the written form retained while the spoken substitute varies by venue; this supports section 6's name-magic design matrix keeping 'written form / permitted spoken form / place' as independent columns, and the coupled politeness-taboo and naming-system files must not collapse them into one global taboo.
audits.limits: The mishnah is a rabbinic compilation (c. 200 CE per the entry); the Wikisource page is marked 'לא בדוק' (not proofread) and displays three textual versions with minor variance, so the citation is to the displayed standard text, not a named manuscript. The English gloss is this worker's, not Danby's wording (Danby 1933 not directly inspected; a Sefaria HTML/API attempt returned only JavaScript chrome and was abandoned, not ground down). Nothing here recovers an Iron Age pronunciation; corroboration below itself notes the pronunciation was 'forgotten' with 'no trace' after 70 CE. All entry bytes remain as hashed at baseline; no knowledge errata asserted by this worker.

audits.corroboration_1_locator: Section 'YHWH' (qere perpetuum passage) and section 'The Name' (Temple pronunciation passage citing Soṭah vii. 6); also section 'Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh' (post-70 CE passage)
audits.corroboration_1_excerpt: Adonai was to be read (as a 'ḳeri perpetuum') instead of Yhwh ... The pronunciation of the written Name was used only by the priests in the Temple ... outside the Temple they used the title 'Adonai'.
audits.corroboration_2_citation: Same article, sections 'YHWH' and 'Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh' - the no-recovered-pronunciation limit
audits.corroboration_2_locator: Section 'YHWH' first paragraph and section 'Ehyeh-Asher-Ehyeh' opening
audits.corroboration_2_excerpt: 'Jehovah' ... is a philological impossibility ... the true pronunciation was forgotten by them ... there remained no trace of knowledge as to the pronunciation of the Name.
audits.corroboration_2_note: Corroboration only, not verification: this is an early twentieth-century reference-work compilation (the entry itself so labels it), used for the standard description of the reading substitutes and the 'Jehovah' caveat; the mishnah text quoted in the main audit is the primary reading. Excerpts stitched with ellipses from the retrieved article text; wording otherwise verbatim.

audits.question: Check priestly garment terminology and the evidential status of the cited biblical prescription; distinguish a dated transmitted text and its translation from excavated dress or a uniform for all Israelites.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/israel-ancient-hebrew.md section 7 'Costume and material signature: bigdei kehuna' (lines 118-138): line 122 (bigdei kehuna / Exodus 28's bigdei qodesh; Yoma 7:5 four/eight classification caution), garment table lines 124-133 with per-row Exodus 28 verse citations, line 136 (Leviticus 16:4 linen set, outside this audit's bounded claim), section 1 line 22 (a prescription establishes what a text enjoins, not obedience), line 121 (no excavated ensemble collated)
audits.entry_claim: The entry asserts: (a) 'bigdei kehuna' means priestly garments, while Exodus 28 itself calls the prescribed vestments 'bigdei qodesh' (holy garments); (b) Exodus 28 names the vestments its table cites - ephod with engraved shoulder stones, me'il of tekhelet with bells and pomegranates, ketonet, mitznefet plus sons' migba'ot headgear, avnet sash, mikhnesei vad linen drawers, doubled hoshen mishpat with twelve named stones, and the gold tzitz plate inscribed with the divine name; (c) the prescription is addressed to Aaron and his sons for sanctuary service, not a garment rule for all Israelites; (d) the four ordinary-priest / eight high-priest garment classification is explicit only in Mishnah Yoma 7:5, a later rabbinic schema, and the whole complex is T-layer transmitted prescription (here JPS 1917 at Mechon-Mamre) - not excavated dress and not evidence of compliance.
audits.source_citation: The Holy Scriptures According to the Masoretic Text (Jewish Publication Society, 1917), Exodus 28:1-43, Hebrew (pointed) with English on facing display, at Mechon-Mamre - the edition the entry itself cites for this chapter
audits.source_locator: Exodus 28:1, 28:3 (addressees 'Aaron ... and his sons ... minister unto Me in the priest's office'); 28:2 and 28:4 ('holy garments' / בִגְדֵי-קֹדֶשׁ and the garment list); 28:35 (bells' sound 'that he die not'); 28:36 ('HOLY TO THE LORD' / קֹדֶשׁ לַיהוָה plate); 28:39-43 (linen tunic, mitre, girdle; sons' tunics, girdles, head-tires; linen breeches)
audits.source_excerpt: a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe, and a tunic of chequer work, a mitre, and a girdle; and they shall make holy garments for Aaron thy brother, and his sons
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL public HTTP GET of the entry-cited Mechon-Mamre Exodus 28 page (JPS 1917 Hebrew-English); full chapter 28:1-43 extracted in both scripts
audits.basis: Every bounded component is checked against the chapter the entry cites: 'holy garments' for Aaron and his sons appears verbatim at 28:2/28:4 (entry claim a); the table-row terms ketonet, mikhnesei vad, avnet, mitznefet/migba'ot, me'il with bells, ephod with shoulder stones, hoshen mishpat with twelve named stones, and tzitz engraved with the divine name all occur in the retrieved verses (claim b); 28:1-4 scopes the prescription to the priesthood 'from among the children of Israel', the laity's role being to contribute materials (28:5-9), supporting claim (c) as textual scope, not a social claim.
audits.coupling_implication: Confirms the entry's costume surface as a permissions system anchored in a transmitted prescription: named garment terms, materials, engraved names, audible movement and authorized office are all prescription-side couplings, so culture-material/ritual-garments.md and material-culture-inference-method.md couplings must keep prescription != practice and priests != all Israelites when handing options to lore-shokunin.
audits.limits: The displayed Hebrew carries full Masoretic pointing - a medieval vocalization layer on a transmitted text, presented in a modern printed edition with a 1917 English translation (the 'dated transmitted text and its translation' the question asks to keep distinct); no excavated priestly garment, Iron Age object or image was retrieved here, and the entry itself collates none. Verse wording establishes the prescription's scope and terms, not historical observance. The four/eight classification is corroborated below from Mishnah Yoma 7:5, not from Exodus 28; Leviticus 16:4 and the Ketef Hinnom amulets are entry anchors not re-verified in this audit and remain outside the bounded claim.
audits.corroboration_1_citation: Mishnah, Seder Moed, Yoma 7:5 - Hebrew text (unpointed, pointed, and Maimonides-codex versions displayed) with commentaries, Hebrew Wikisource public-domain transcription
audits.corroboration_1_locator: Yoma 7:5, opening sentence and garment enumeration
audits.corroboration_1_excerpt: כהן גדול משמש בשמונה כלים, וההדיוט בארבעה - 'The high priest serves in eight garments, the common [priest] in four': tunic, breeches, turban, sash; adding breastplate, ephod, robe, plate.
audits.corroboration_1_note: Confirms the entry's attribution of the 4/8 classification to Yoma 7:5 as an explicit Mishnah-level schema (rabbinic, c. 200 CE, post-destruction recollection - per the entry's own caution, not a dated excavation inventory). Page marked 'לא בדוק' (not proofread); Hebrew quoted, gloss this worker's, not Danby's. The page's Tosafot Yom Tov commentary also records that the Torah calls the ordinary priest's headgear migba'at while the sages say mitznefet, matching the entry's mitznefet/migba'ot row distinction.
